entities.name: Colorado
entities.funFact: Colorado has 58 mountains taller than 14,000 feet. Climbers call them fourteeners.
entities.funFactDetail: Denver sits exactly one mile above the sea, so people call it the Mile High City. On the steps of the state capitol there is a line carved into the stone marking that height. Water is so high up here that rivers flowing out of Colorado end up in the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Gulf of California.

entities.name: Florida
entities.funFact: Florida is a peninsula, which means water wraps around it on three sides.
entities.funFactDetail: The Atlantic Ocean is on the east, the Gulf of Mexico is on the west, and only the top edge touches land. That is why Florida has more coastline than any other state except Alaska. The southern tip is so warm and wet that it holds the Everglades, a river of grass that moves slower than you walk.

entities.name: Texas
entities.funFact: Texas is so wide that El Paso is closer to California than to Houston.
entities.funFactDetail: Driving across Texas takes longer than driving across all six New England states in a row. It was its own country for nine years before joining the United States, which is why people call it the Lone Star State.

entities.name: Alaska
entities.funFact: Alaska is the biggest state, and in summer the sun barely sets in the far north.
entities.funFactDetail: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas. Its capital, Juneau, has no roads leading in or out. You reach it by boat or plane. Denali, the tallest mountain in North America, stands here at 20,310 feet.

entities.name: Hawaii
entities.funFact: Hawaii is made of volcanoes, and it is still growing today.
entities.funFactDetail: Every Hawaiian island began as lava on the ocean floor that piled up until it broke the surface. Kilauea erupts often, adding new land. Hawaii is the only state made entirely of islands.

entities.name: Maine
entities.funFact: The sun rises over Maine before anywhere else in the United States.
entities.funFactDetail: Maine sticks out farther east than any other state, so morning light lands there first. It touches only one other state, New Hampshire. Most of Maine is forest, and its rocky coast is dotted with hundreds of small islands.

entities.name: Michigan
entities.funFact: Michigan is shaped like a mitten, and it touches four of the five Great Lakes.
entities.funFactDetail: The lower part really does look like a left hand in a mitten, and people from Michigan point to spots on their palm to show where they live. The upper part, called the Upper Peninsula, is connected by a five-mile bridge.

entities.name: Louisiana
entities.funFact: The Mississippi River dumps its mud in Louisiana, building new land as it goes.
entities.funFactDetail: After traveling 2,300 miles, the Mississippi spreads into a delta shaped a bit like a bird's foot. Much of southern Louisiana is swamp and bayou, slow water full of cypress trees, herons, and alligators.

entities.name: California
entities.funFact: California holds the highest and lowest places in the lower 48 states, and they are close together.
entities.funFactDetail: Mount Whitney rises to 14,505 feet. Badwater Basin in Death Valley sits 282 feet below sea level. They are only about 85 miles apart. More people live in California than in any other state.

entities.name: New York
entities.funFact: New York City is the biggest city in the country, but it is not the state capital.
entities.funFactDetail: The capital is Albany, about 150 miles up the Hudson River. Lawmakers picked a quieter inland city on purpose. Upstate New York is full of mountains, farms, and the Finger Lakes, long skinny lakes carved by glaciers.

entities.name: Arizona
entities.funFact: The Grand Canyon is a mile deep, and the Colorado River carved it out slowly.
entities.funFactDetail: Water cut through rock for millions of years. Each stripe you see in the canyon wall is a different layer of time. The bottom rocks are almost two billion years old.

entities.name: Kansas
entities.funFact: Kansas sits almost exactly in the middle of the country.
entities.funFactDetail: The geographic center of the 48 connected states is near Lebanon, Kansas. Kansas is famous for wheat and for thunderstorms that roll across wide open plains where you can see weather coming from far away.

entities.name: Washington
entities.funFact: One side of Washington is a rainforest and the other side is nearly a desert.
entities.funFactDetail: The Cascade Mountains catch clouds coming off the ocean. Rain falls on the west side, so much that moss hangs off the trees. By the time the air crosses the mountains it is dry, so eastern Washington gets little rain.

entities.name: Minnesota
entities.funFact: Minnesota calls itself the land of 10,000 lakes. It actually has closer to 12,000.
entities.funFactDetail: Glaciers scraped across this land during the last ice age and left thousands of dents that filled with water. The Mississippi River starts here too, at Lake Itasca, where it is small enough to step across.

entities.name: Nevada
entities.funFact: Nevada is the driest state, and rain that falls there never reaches the ocean.
entities.funFactDetail: Most of Nevada sits in the Great Basin. Rivers flow into valleys and lakes with no way out, so the water sits and evaporates. The land goes up and down in long mountain ranges like a rumpled blanket.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Colorado. It is the neat rectangle high in the Rocky Mountains, with Kansas on its flat eastern side.
questions.detailExplanation: Colorado is one of only three states drawn with straight lines on every side. Mapmakers used lines of latitude and longitude instead of rivers or mountains. Look for the rectangle sitting right where the plains stop and the Rockies begin.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Colorado?
questions.shortExplanation: Denver is the capital. It grew during a gold rush and sits exactly one mile above sea level.
questions.detailExplanation: Miners came looking for gold in 1858, and the town they built at the edge of the mountains became Denver. It was already the biggest city around when Colorado became a state, so it kept the capital.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Florida, the long piece of land reaching down into the ocean.
questions.detailExplanation: A piece of land with water on three sides is called a peninsula. Florida is one of the easiest shapes to find on a map of the United States because it points straight down toward the Caribbean Sea.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Florida?
questions.shortExplanation: Tallahassee is the capital, up in the panhandle. It was picked because it sat halfway between the two biggest towns of the time.
questions.detailExplanation: In 1824 the two important cities were Pensacola and St. Augustine, far apart on opposite coasts. Riders set out from each one and met in the middle, near an old Native American town. That meeting spot became Tallahassee.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Texas, the huge state at the bottom of the country with a curved bottom edge.
questions.detailExplanation: The bottom edge of Texas curves because it follows the Rio Grande, the river that forms the border with Mexico. Rivers make wiggly borders, straight lines make neat ones.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Texas?
questions.shortExplanation: Austin is the capital, even though Houston, Dallas, and San Antonio are all bigger.
questions.detailExplanation: Capitals are not always the biggest city. Austin was chosen when Texas was still its own country because it sat near the middle, where lawmakers from every direction could reach it.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Alaska. On most maps it is tucked into a corner so it fits, but it is really way up northwest, past Canada.
questions.detailExplanation: Alaska is so big and so far away that mapmakers shrink it and move it into an empty corner. If it were drawn in its true place and size, it would take up a huge part of the page.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Alaska?
questions.shortExplanation: Juneau is the capital, and no road reaches it. You arrive by boat or plane.
questions.detailExplanation: Juneau is squeezed between steep mountains and the sea, with glaciers behind it. Building a highway through that ice and rock has never been worth the cost, so it stays a capital you can only fly or sail to.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Hawaii, a chain of islands out in the Pacific Ocean.
questions.detailExplanation: Hawaii sits about 2,400 miles from California, which is why maps show it in a little box. It is the only state that is not attached to North America at all.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Hawaii?
questions.shortExplanation: Honolulu is the capital. It sits on Oahu, which is not even the biggest island.
questions.detailExplanation: Honolulu grew around a deep, protected harbor where ships could safely stop. A good harbor mattered more than island size, so the busiest port became the capital.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Maine, the state in the far top right corner, farther east than any other.
questions.detailExplanation: Because Earth spins toward the east, the easternmost land sees the sun first. Maine's rocky point at Quoddy Head gets the very first sunrise in the country.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Maine?
questions.shortExplanation: Augusta is the capital. It sits inland on the Kennebec River, away from the open sea.
questions.detailExplanation: Coastal towns were easy to attack from the water, so many states put their capitals a little way up a river. Augusta is far enough upstream to be safe but still reachable by boat.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Michigan, the state shaped like a mitten with a thumb sticking out.
questions.detailExplanation: Michigan comes in two pieces held apart by water. The Great Lakes around it hold about one fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Michigan?
questions.shortExplanation: Lansing is the capital. Detroit is much bigger, but it sat right on the border.
questions.detailExplanation: Detroit is across a narrow river from Canada, and after a war people worried it was too exposed. Lawmakers moved the capital to Lansing, which at the time was little more than forest in the middle of the state.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Louisiana. Look for the boot shape at the bottom of the Mississippi River, with a ragged coast.
questions.detailExplanation: The coast looks torn because the river keeps dropping mud there, building marshes and channels. Land and water trade places constantly, so no map of Louisiana stays right for long.

questions.shortExplanation: This is California, the long state running down the whole west coast.
questions.detailExplanation: California stretches almost 800 miles from top to bottom. Because it is so long, the north can be cool and rainy on the same day the south is hot and dry.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of California?
questions.shortExplanation: Sacramento is the capital. It was the gold rush supply town where two rivers meet.
questions.detailExplanation: When gold was found in 1848, boats carried miners up the river as far as Sacramento. Everything and everyone passed through, so it became the natural place to run the new state from.

questions.shortExplanation: This is New York. It reaches from the Atlantic coast all the way up to two Great Lakes.
questions.detailExplanation: That reach was worth a lot. The Erie Canal was dug across the state so boats could travel from the ocean to the Great Lakes, and New York City became the busiest port in the country.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of New York?
questions.shortExplanation: Albany is the capital, not New York City. It sits upriver on the Hudson.
questions.detailExplanation: Albany is one of the oldest towns in the country and sat in the middle of the state's trade routes. Lawmakers also liked keeping government away from the crowds and money of the big city.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Arizona. Its western edge bends along the Colorado River, the same river that cut the Grand Canyon.
questions.detailExplanation: Arizona's straight top and right edges were drawn by people, but the wavy left edge was drawn by water. When a border follows a river, you can read the land's story right off the map.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Arizona?
questions.shortExplanation: Phoenix is the capital. A city grew in the desert because old canals brought water there.
questions.detailExplanation: The Hohokam people dug canals across this valley more than a thousand years ago. Later settlers cleaned them out and used them again, which is why a city rose from the desert and took the name of a bird reborn.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Kansas, sitting almost dead center. Look for the small notch cut out of its top right corner.
questions.detailExplanation: That notch is the Missouri River. Kansas is a rectangle everywhere the border was drawn with a ruler, and bent only where a river got in the way.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Washington, the top left corner of the lower 48, with Oregon just below it.
questions.detailExplanation: The ragged bite out of its northwest coast is Puget Sound, a maze of deep water channels left behind by glaciers. Seattle sits along it.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Minnesota. It has a little bump on top that pokes farther north than any other state in the lower 48.
questions.detailExplanation: That bump is called the Northwest Angle. It exists because of an old map mistake about where the Mississippi River started, and nobody ever redrew the line.

questions.shortExplanation: This is Nevada. Its slanted southwest edge presses right up against California.
questions.detailExplanation: That diagonal line was drawn to follow the Sierra Nevada mountains, so California could keep the gold country on the western slope. Nevada got the dry basin on the other side.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Minnesota?
questions.shortExplanation: Saint Paul is the capital. It sits right next to Minneapolis, and together they are called the Twin Cities.
questions.detailExplanation: Saint Paul grew at the last spot steamboats could reach going up the Mississippi. Minneapolis grew a few miles upstream at a waterfall that powered flour mills. Two reasons, two cities, side by side.
